The walk rate (7.2%, 69th percentile) is the number to watch; he doesn't have enough pure stuff to survive prolonged command lapses, so the margin for error is thinner than the ERA suggests. ValuCast projects him for a 3.25 ERA over 181.2 innings with 185 strikeouts at Cleveland — a genuine mid-rotation producer, as long as he keeps the ball where it needs to be.

ValuCast projects him at .273/.344/.429, a useful profile if the barrel rate ever ticks up, but right now he's a well-disciplined hitter whose bat-to-ball skill outpaces his ability to do damage with the contact he makes.

800060_hitter.text: Xavier Isaac is a first baseman built around a walk rate that jumps off the page — 19% at AA this year, which translates to a projected 13.1% at the MLB level against a league average of 8.5%, and his 14 home runs in 268 PA back up a real power threat. Projection sees a bench or platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot — the approach and power are genuine, but the contact rate has to prove it can hold. 800125_pitcher.text: Fernando Perez is a 22-year-old starter wrestling with command at AA—his 11.4 BB/9 on the current minor-league line is a severe control leak that dwarfs his strikeout rate of 5.0 K/9. 800169_hitter.text: Aroon Escobar is a 21-year-old contact-and-approach profile at AA — the kind of hitter who makes the ball count when he swings but doesn't hurt you much when he connects. The problem is the other side of the ledger: a .098 ISO in the minors that translates to .103 equivalent — well below the .150 MLB average — and with 19 steals doing some of the lifting, the bat doesn't carry its own weight yet. 800176_hitter.text: Carlos Sanchez is a contact-over-strikeout left-handed hitter making hard contact in the minors—.307 average with .508 SLG over 310 PA at A+—but his swing-and-miss remains a real problem at 23.9 K%. 800198_hitter.text: Cristofer Torin is a 21-year-old SS who makes contact at an elite clip — his 12% K-rate at AA translates to roughly 16.7% against MLB pitching, well below the 22.0% league average — and that's genuinely the carrying tool here. 800208_hitter.text: Axiel Plaz is a 20-year-old catcher hitting like the best bat in the A+ pool — .317/.396/.519 with a .202 ISO in 218 PA isn't a fluke line, it's a real contact-and-pop combination that grades as hit-tool elite against peers. Projected as a bench or platoon piece with a reserve floor and two to three years of development runway, though the projection carries more upside than today's A+ value captures — if the hit tool is real at a premium position, the ceiling conversation opens up.

800281_hitter.text: Roynier Hernandez is a contact-heavy left-handed hitter working from a disciplined approach—elite 93rd percentile in batting average (.304) paired with a 12.1% walk rate that sits above league average. The translation to MLB shows modest erosion across the board—K% rising to 20.0%, ISO dropping to .12—leaving a bench-or-platoon ceiling in the 85% probability band. 800286_pitcher.text: Wellington Aracena is a high-strikeout, poor-control starter prospect operating well above league-average whiff rates but constrained by walk management. 800305_hitter.text: Jesús Báez is a 21-year-old shortstop built on raw power—ISO of .242 in 243 PA at A+—but undermined by a swing-and-miss problem that will limit his hit tool and overall impact. The main flaw is approach: a grade-20 on plate discipline and a 91st-percentile strikeout rate signal he will struggle to put the ball in play consistently enough to profile as more than organizational depth. 800306_hitter.text: Jansel Luis is a 21-year-old third baseman whose current bat is built around power (.164 ISO, 61st percentile) but undermined by contact issues—he's striking out in 26.9% of his at-bats while walking in only 5.4%, ranking in the bottom 3rd on approach discipline. 800325_hitter.text: Luis Lara is a 21-year-old contact-and-patience machine at AAA, and the bat-to-ball ability is genuine — a 14% strikeout rate against a 16% walk rate over 328 PA is the kind of discipline you almost never see from a prospect his age. His AAA line of .327/.437/.463 translates to roughly a 17.5% K rate and 12.1% walk rate in MLB context, both comfortably better than league average, and the 21 stolen bases tell you the athleticism is real. The one honest question mark is the power ceiling: a .136 ISO at this level with a MLB-equivalent .124 suggests he's a hitter who makes everyone look, not a guy who punishes mistakes — and whether he grows into average game power or stays a slash-and-run profile is the thing to watch. ValuCast projects him as an everyday regular, and he's rising +1.4 in the last three days in rankings.

800338_pitcher.text: Franklin Gómez is a 20-year-old left-hander who gets outs by not walking anyone — his 2.8 BB/9 across 58 innings at A+ puts him in the 87th percentile of his peer pool, and that command is the engine behind a 3.10 ERA and 1.20 WHIP that read as genuinely clean, not fluky. The strikeout rate (10.2 K/9 in the minors, translating to a roughly league-average 8.1 at the MLB equivalent level) is solid but not a carrying tool on its own, so the command has to keep doing the heavy lifting as he climbs. ValuCast has him rising — up +9 spots over the last three days — and projects a multi-inning or setup role as the ceiling, with a floor of depth arm; the 85% probability of being a useful MLB arm is the honest read on a guy whose stuff may profile better in shorter bursts than in a rotation.

800344_pitcher.text: Sean Paul Liñan is a high-velocity bat-missing arm operating well ahead of his age curve in A+ ball. His 12.9 K/9 and 22.3% K-BB% rank in the 91st and 92nd percentiles respectively, the cleanest calling cards of a young pitcher with real strikeout potential. The fatal hitch is his ERA of 6.44 paired with a 1.32 WHIP—control and command have not kept pace with his stuff, and early returns suggest significant damage on contact when he misses in the zone. The sample is fresh and live at 43.3 innings, but translating to MLB equivalents drops that K-BB% to 13.7%, roughly league average, which is the sobering floor this profile must clear.

800387_hitter.text: Fernando Peguero is a 21-year-old right fielder whose swing-and-miss profile is dominating his plate approach: over a 151 PA AAA+AA-equivalent sample, he strikes out in 25.7% of his looks while walking in just 9.4%, creating a heavily strikeout-dependent floor. His ISO translated to .116, well below the league average of .150, which means when he does make contact, he generates little power. The current 59 PA minor-league sample is live but shallow; strikeout rates and power production at his age warrant another 100+ PA to trust whether this is a repeatable profile or early-season noise.

800393_hitter.text: Yeremy Cabrera is a 20-year-old left-handed hitter with a disciplined approach that outpaces his ability to convert contact into impact—a classic high-strikeout, low-power profile at an early stage. His 12.3% BB% grades well relative to his cohort (57th percentile), but a 27.7% K% and .052 ISO (3rd percentile) reveal a hitter who takes pitches he can't drive, leaving him with a .62 OPS across 130 PA at A+. The primary risk is the power deficit: even accounting for age and level, there's no bat-speed or force signal to suggest he'll generate the impact needed for regular opportunity. This is a thin sample on an organizational depth trajectory, so how his bat develops over the next two years remains largely uncertain.

800406_hitter.text: Aron Estrada is a 21-year-old second baseman who can hit and has real pop, but walks almost nobody — and that's the problem. At AA in 2026 over 277 PA, he's slashing .271/.312/.473 with 13 home runs and an .202 ISO, and his K% (18%) and contact quality translate to a K-BB spread that won't play against better pitching. The MLB-equivalent read confirms the shape: his strikeout rate comes in below the 22.0% league average at 21.3%, but his walk rate (6.3% translated) sits well short of the 8.5% MLB mean, and it's that 5% walk rate in-park — third percentile among his peer pool — that caps his ceiling. ValuCast projects him as a bench or platoon bat, with 85% probability he lands there and only 5% for a regular role, and he's cooled five spots in the ValuCast rankings over the last three days.

800419_hitter.text: Jeral Perez is a 21-year-old shortstop bat at AA struggling to make consistent contact, with a .177 AVG and 27.0% K% over his active 237-PA sample. He is walking at a respectable 10.5% rate, but the 6th-percentile OBP (.274) and near-total lack of gap power (0.101 ISO, 21st percentile) leave him with a .552 OPS that ranks in the bottom 5%. The core problem is hit tool — strikeouts are eating up at-bats and neither the walk rate nor the isolated power is compensating. 800421_hitter.text: Marvin Alcantara is a 21-year-old contact-first middle infielder who makes enough contact to stay interesting but hasn't yet shown the power or patience to make it count at AA. His 17% K% translates to a projected 20.6% at the MLB level — actually below the 22.0% league average — so the bat-to-ball is real. What isn't real yet is the impact: a .127 ISO and .288 OBP over 288 PA, with the MLB-equivalent ISO projecting at .118 against a .150 league average, tells you the gap between contact and damage is the whole problem. Fifteen stolen bases show he can create value elsewhere, and the projection does see more upside than today's line, with a 55% shot at a bench or platoon role — but until there's more pull-side authority, he profiles as a depth piece whose outcome hinges entirely on whether the power develops. ValuCast has him trending up +1.0 in the last three days in rankings.

800449_hitter.text: Thomas Sosa is a left-handed right fielder with raw power but a swing-and-miss problem that is eroding his offensive floor. His ISO ranks 62nd percentile at .167, but his .219 AVG and 23.4% K rate signal a hitter whose contact rate cannot support that power—his OBP sits at .286, 11th percentile. The main risk is approach discipline: his 7.9% BB rate ranks only 17th percentile against a league average of 8.5%, meaning he's chasing and missing without generating the walks needed to compensate for strikeouts. ValuCast projects him toward organizational depth with a bench/platoon likelihood of 58%, which reflects upside over his current 252 PA showing but meaningful execution risk over the next one to two years.

800473_hitter.text: Jefferson Rojas is a 21-year-old third baseman who can actually hit — .291/.356/.498 in 278 AA plate appearances, with a 17% K% and .207 ISO that hold up under translation (20.5% and .154 in MLB-equivalent terms, both right around league average or better). ValuCast projects a low-end everyday regular as the ceiling, with a reserve floor if the approach doesn't develop — and he's cooled slightly in rankings over the last three days, down 0.7 in score.

800537_pitcher.text: Christian Zazueta is a 21-year-old right-hander doing something genuinely rare at AA: missing bats at a 12.4 K/9 clip while barely issuing any free passes — 2.0 BB/9, a 30% K-BB%, and a 0.90 WHIP across 53.7 combined innings at A+ and AA in 2026. 800540_hitter.text: Hector Osorio is a high-contact, discerning hitter who controls the strike zone at an elite level — his current A+ sample shows 9.9% K and 12.7% BB%, both among the top percentiles of the ValuCast hitter pool. 800543_hitter.text: Josue De Paula is a 21-year-old left-handed hitter doing something genuinely rare at Double-A: hitting for average and power while barely striking out. The catch is the 5.6 ERA, which tells you the command isn't yet converting to consistent run prevention, and a 33rd-percentile K/9 in this pool means he doesn't miss enough bats to paper over mistakes. Current sample is live and sizable enough to trust, but the command limitations will need to narrow for him to reach beyond organizational depth.

The MLB-equivalent translation puts his K/9 at 9.1 against a 3.8 BB/9, both roughly league average at the big-league level — fine for a reliever, probably not enough runway for a rotation. The projection has him as a multi-inning or setup arm, with the floor being depth, and that feels right: the miss is an 80, the command is a 45, and until he narrows that gap, the bullpen is where this resolves.

805953_hitter.text: Anthony Huezo is a 20-year-old left-handed hitter generating genuine power—.298 ISO in the 98th percentile—but strangled by swing-and-miss; his 31.3% strikeout rate ranks in the 18th percentile and will cap his floor hard if it doesn't improve. His .909 OPS on 268 plate appearances is real and translates to solid impact, yet the contact collapse is the legitimate risk: when the strikeouts run that high, the hit tool (.259 AVG, 67th percentile) can't recover the value. ValuCast projects him as organizational depth with upside, arriving in two to three years, but the strikeout problem is the gate he must pass through first.

806010_pitcher.text: Barrett Kent is a young starter with elite early command results but a control leak that requires monitoring—27.3 innings of 1.98 ERA and 7.2 K/9 mask a 5.3 BB/9 rate (36th percentile) that sits well above MLB average when translated. This is a stale, thin starter sample from prior-season A-ball; confidence in any read here is low given the 27-inning workload and lack of recent activity.

806046_pitcher.text: Alex Clemmey is a 20-year-old lefty who can miss bats but can't find the zone — and right now, the second half of that sentence is the whole story. At AA this year, he's walking 6.1 per nine across 72.3 innings, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 5.3 BB/9 against a league average of 3.2 — that's a command profile that sits near the bottom of the prospect pitcher pool. The strikeout rate is real enough (9.5 K/9 in AA, translates to roughly league-average 8.1), but a K-BB% that ranks 24th percentile against peers tells you the misses aren't beating the free passes by nearly enough. ValuCast projects a multi-inning or setup reliever ceiling, with a depth arm as the floor, and he's rising nine spots in the rankings over the last three days — but the path there runs straight through fixing the walk rate, because nothing else moves until that does.

806061_hitter.text: Isaiah Drake is a left-handed hitter showing a pull-heavy, power-first approach that hasn't yet translated into consistent contact or on-base skill at A+ ball. The projection floor is organizational depth with a two-to-three-year timeline; current performance suggests medium risk to that floor given the early-stage strikeout profile.

806071_hitter.text: Jonny Farmelo is a 21-year-old center fielder who walks nearly as often as he strikes out — 16% BB%, 25% K% at A+ — and that discipline is carrying real pop behind it, with an .855 OPS and .207 ISO through 338 PA. 806146_hitter.text: George Lombard Jr. is a walk machine at 21, and that's not a small thing — his 16% BB rate at AAA+AA translates to a 12.3% MLB-equivalent walk rate against an 8.5% league average, which is the floor his entire offensive game stands on. 806191_hitter.text: Tai Peete is a high-leverage power bat in early A+ ball who trades contact for explosive slugging — his .256 ISO ranks 95th percentile among hitters with 100+ PA, but a 31.4% strikeout rate undercuts the hit tool and approach. 806198_hitter.text: Cooper Pratt is a 21-year-old shortstop whose future hinges almost entirely on whether he can hit enough to stay in a lineup — and right now, the answer is probably not. The ValuCast projection over 289 PA has him at .220/.302/.312 with a .614 OPS, which is fringe-roster production at best for a corner bat and outright replacement-level if you're asking him to carry a premium defensive position. What keeps him interesting is the sprint speed — 79th percentile at 28.4 ft/s — which explains the 13 projected steals and gives him a real non-bat tool; a guy who can run like that and play shortstop has a job description, it just requires the bat to be functional. Four home runs in 289 trips tells you the power isn't coming to bail him out, so the question is whether he develops enough contact and on-base ability to profile as a speedy utility piece. Medium confidence from ValuCast here, and honestly that feels right for a 21-year-old with a thin MLB track record and a profile that lives or dies by a skill — hitting — that isn't there yet.

806210_hitter.text: Alfonsin Rosario is a 22-year-old right fielder built around one thing: raw power, and a lot of it.
